introduction: “Consider thy state when asleep. Verily, I say, this phenomenon is the most mysterious of the signs of God amongst men.” Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá use the dream for two purposes. It is an argument: the sleeper’s senses are shut, yet he sees, hears and travels, which shows a spirit that does not depend on the body. And it is an experience their correspondents kept writing about, so the readings give practical guidance. Dreams are of three kinds: true visions, dreams that need interpretation because the heart’s own impressions are mixed in, and the confused product of nerves and digestion. A true dream is a private gift; it is not to be told about in meetings, and one that would cause harm is not to be acted on. “Lay aside the dream and seize hold of” the Book. Scripture is full of dreams, and Joseph, Jacob, Daniel, Solomon and Paul appear here; so do its warnings, from Jeremiah, Ecclesiastes, Deuteronomy and Ben Sira. Homer’s two gates make the readings’ distinction; Aristotle, Mercutio, Bacon and Hobbes speak for doubt; and Abraham’s dream of sacrifice is the case that tests every rule.
questions: The sleeper sees with closed eyes. How strong do you find this as evidence for the soul, given that the readings also say many dreams are mere fancy?
“Three kinds of visions or dreams.” By what marks do the readings tell them apart? Which mark could you apply yourself?
A believer was told to keep her dream “private to herself.” Why? What happened to Joseph when he told his?
“If thou art not seeing dreams … be thou not sad … A wakeful eye is acceptable.” What is the wakeful eye, and why might it be worth more?
“Lay aside the dream and seize hold of” the Book. Hobbes says a dream gives the dreamer no claim on anyone else. What place does that leave for dreams in a religious life?

outside.why: Sleep is “the most mysterious of the signs of God amongst men.” Elihu: in a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men; then he openeth the ears of men.
A thing seen in a dream comes to pass long afterwards. Hamlet: there are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy.
One dream comes true exactly; another “has absolutely no result.” Penelope: there are two gates through which these unsubstantial fancies proceed; the one is of horn, and the other ivory.
Aristotle allowed only one gate: most so-called prophetic dreams are to be classed as mere coincidences. What evidence would distinguish a true dream from a coincidence? Do the readings offer any?
A prayer that the inner eye may tell truthful dreams from untruthful. Of Daniel it is said: he had understanding in all visions and dreams.
Jeremiah draws a line of his own: the prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat?
The dream world “is evidence of a realm wherein no beginning or end” can be seen. Jacob at Bethel: he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven.
“That which we behold in a dream … sometimes later takes place.” Joseph’s sheaves, dreamed at seventeen, were fulfilled when his brothers bowed to him in Egypt.
In sleep the senses are stilled, “yet the spirit continues its journey.” The Qur’án: Allah receiveth men’s souls at the time of their death, and that soul which dieth not yet in its sleep.
His eye does not see, “but, nevertheless, he does see.” The Song of Songs: I sleep, but my heart waketh.

“In the world of dreams the soul sees when the eyes are closed.” Mercutio would have none of it: I talk of dreams, which are the children of an idle brain, begot of nothing but vain fantasy. The readings grant that some dreams are exactly this. How does that affect their argument from dreaming to the soul?
The body lies as dead while the spirit moves. Prospero reverses the picture and makes waking life the dream: we are such stuff as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with a sleep.
As in dreams the soul travels while the body is still, so at death it is unaffected. Shelley on Keats: he hath awakened from the dream of life.
The psalmist: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.
Two meet in a dream; one remembers and one forgets. Jacob on waking: surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not.
“The human heart resembleth a mirror.” Zhuangzi: when the perfect man employs his mind, it is a mirror. It responds to what is before it, but does not retain it.

Revelations are of two kinds, through images and intermediaries or without them. Numbers makes the same distinction: I will speak unto him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so; with him will I speak mouth to mouth.
“Divine vision on the Day of God is mentioned in all the holy scriptures.” Joel, quoted at Pentecost: your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.
Three kinds of dreams; the first comes of nerves or stomach and is “of no use whatever.” Ecclesiastes: in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities.
The second kind needs interpreting. Joseph in prison: do not interpretations belong to God?
“Confused dreams and fancies are imaginations.” Pharaoh’s counsellors, unable to read his dream, used the same category: jumbled dreams!
“Whatever is revealed as true in the world of dreams is a truthful dream.” The Qur’án: Allah hath fulfilled the vision for His messenger in very truth.
A revelation received in vision “later comes to pass.” Paul at Troas: there stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.

Spiritual dreams are “discoveries of the heart.” Theseus: lovers and madmen have such seething brains, such shaping fantasies, that apprehend more than cool reason ever comprehends. Is he dismissing such apprehension or, without meaning to, describing it?
“Give thanks unto God for having revealed unto thee, in visions, the mysteries of His Kingdom.” Cornelius, a soldier who prayed: he saw in a vision evidently an angel of God coming in to him.
One who recites with love “will witness in his dreams whatever he hath desired.” Solomon at Gibeon: the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night: and God said, Ask what I shall give thee.
Before a decision to move: pray, sleep, and heed what is inspired in a dream. Joseph of Nazareth: the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and flee into Egypt.

Ben Sira would have advised against the method: whoso regardeth dreams is like him that catcheth at a shadow, and followeth after the wind. What safeguards surround this counsel in the other readings?
A disturbing dream: recite a prayer and let it go. Pilate’s wife: I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him.
A believer “should not mention her dream to anyone.” Joseph told his, and his brothers said: behold, this dreamer cometh. Come now therefore, and let us slay him.
Dreams that would cause harm are not to be acted on or even told. Jeremiah: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the Lord.

The hardest case in scripture: Abraham said, O my dear son, I have seen in a dream that I must sacrifice thee. How do the readings’ rules (no acting on a dream that would cause harm; the Book above the dream) bear on a story like this one?
“If thou art not seeing dreams … be thou not sad … A wakeful eye is acceptable.” Paul: now it is high time to awake out of sleep.
A dream fulfilled two years later; a problem solved in sleep. The returning exiles could hardly believe their waking: we were like them that dream.
True visions, dreams needing interpretation, and confused ones. Daniel to the king: there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets.
“Whatever is spoken and heard during the day is seen in the world of dreams.” Bacon on why people credit dreams and prophecies: men mark when they hit, and never mark when they miss.

“Lay aside the dream and seize hold of that which the All-Bountiful hath revealed in His Book.” Deuteronomy on a dreamer of dreams whose sign comes true but who leads away from God: thou shalt not hearken unto him.

Hobbes states the public difficulty: to say he hath spoken to him in a Dream, is no more then to say he dreamed that God spake to him. The last reading agrees that a dream gives no authority over others. What, then, is a true dream good for?

quran-jumbled-dreams.text: They answered: Jumbled dreams! And we are not knowing in the interpretation of dreams.

quran-fulfilled-the-vision.text: Allah hath fulfilled the vision for His messenger in very truth. Ye shall indeed enter the Inviolable Place of Worship, if Allah will, secure, (having your hair) shaven and cut, not fearing. But He knoweth that which ye know not, and hath given you a near victory beforehand.

kings-ask-what-i-shall-give-thee.text: In Gibeon the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night: and God said, Ask what I shall give thee

matthew-suffered-many-things-in-a-dream.text: When he was set down on the judgment seat, his wife sent unto him, saying, Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him

psalm-like-them-that-dream.text: When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The Lord hath done great things for them

daniel-a-god-in-heaven-that-revealeth-se.text: The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king; But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days

homer-two-gates-of-dreams.text: There are two gates through which these unsubstantial fancies proceed; the one is of horn, and the other ivory. Those that come through the gate of ivory are fatuous, but those from the gate of horn mean something to those that see them
homer-two-gates-of-dreams.author: Homer

aristotle-dreams-mere-coincidences.text: Most [so-called prophetic] dreams are, however, to be classed as mere coincidences

shakespeare-children-of-an-idle-brain.text: I talk of dreams, / Which are the children of an idle brain, / Begot of nothing but vain fantasy, / Which is as thin of substance as the air / And more inconstant than the wind
